groups.title: Server Actions Architecture
groups.question: You are building a 'create post' form in Next.js without writing a separate API endpoint, and the post list must update after saving. Explain how server actions work.

followUps.What server actions are and how they exe: What is a server action and where does it run?
followUps.Form submissions with the action prop: What happens when you pass a server action to a form's action prop?
followUps.Revalidation and cache invalidation afte: Why must you revalidate after a mutation?

evidence.text: A server action is an async function marked use server.
It runs on the server, even when called from a client component or form.
It removes the need for a separate API route for the app's own mutations.

notEnough: Only saying it runs server code.

evidence.text: Submitting the form calls the action on the server with the form data.
It works even before JavaScript loads, which is progressive enhancement.
No manual fetch or submit handler is needed.

notEnough: Only saying the form calls the action.

evidence.text: Pages and data may be cached.
Without revalidation, the UI keeps showing the old data.
Calling revalidatePath or revalidateTag refreshes the affected pages.

groups.title: Validation and Error Handling
groups.question: Users can submit the create-post form with an empty title, and when something fails they see a crash instead of a message. Explain how you would validate and report results.

followUps.Schema validation with Zod in server act: Why validate form data with Zod inside the server action?
followUps.Returning errors and success states from: Why return an error object instead of throwing, and how does the form read it?

evidence.text: Form data reaching the server can be anything, regardless of client checks.
A Zod schema checks the types and shape before using the data.
Zod's errors can be returned to show which field is wrong.
Returning an object with errors or success gives the UI something to display.
Throwing would hit an error boundary instead of showing field messages.
useActionState connects the action's result to the form.

groups.title: Route Handlers for APIs
groups.question: A mobile app and a partner service need to create posts too, not just your own forms. Explain when you would add route handlers and how they read requests.

followUps.Route handlers as REST API endpoints: When would you use a route handler instead of a server action?
followUps.Reading request body and query parameter: How do you read the body and query parameters, and what must you always do with them?

evidence.text: A route.ts file exports functions named after HTTP methods.
Route handlers suit public APIs used by other apps or services.
Server actions are mainly for your own app's forms and mutations.

notEnough: Only saying route handlers are APIs.

evidence.text: The request's JSON body is read from the request object.
Query parameters come from the URL's search params.
All external input must be validated before use.

notEnough: Only saying you read the request.

groups.title: Optimistic UI and Pending States
groups.question: Users click submit twice because nothing shows it is working, likes take a second to appear, and errors only show after the server responds. Explain how you would improve the form experience.

followUps.useFormStatus for pending button states: How does useFormStatus help with the submit button?
followUps.useOptimistic for instant UI feedback: How does useOptimistic make a like appear instantly?
followUps.Zod form validation and client-side erro: Why also run Zod on the client?

evidence.text: useFormStatus reads whether the surrounding form is submitting.
The button can be disabled and show a spinner while pending.
No manual loading state is needed.
useOptimistic shows the expected result immediately.
When the server responds, the real data replaces it.
If the action fails, the optimistic value is dropped.

notEnough: Only saying it updates the UI first.

evidence.text: Client-side checks catch obvious mistakes immediately.
Field-level messages guide users to fix their input.
The server still validates, because client checks can be bypassed.

notEnough: Only saying you validate on the client.
